title: Association of preserved ratio impaired spirometry and restrictive spirometric pattern with incident atrial fibrillation: a cohort study
summary: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is associated with an increased risk of atrial fibrillation (AF). To our knowledge, no studies have examined the association of preserved ratio impaired spirometry (PRISm) or restrictive spirometric pattern (RSP) with incident AF. We included participants without prevalent AF who had incident AF ascertainment and available spirometry and excluded those with airflow limitation. PRISm and RSP were evaluated as binary exposures and as four mutually exclusive spirometric patterns. Missing covariates were handled using multiple imputation by chained equations, and logistic regression estimates were pooled using Rubin’s rules. Sensitivity analyses used an individual lower limit of normal (LLN) for the forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV 1 )/forced vital capacity (FVC) ratio, complete-case analysis, and an alternative smoking model including pack-years and current smoking. A total of 2219 participants were included, with a mean age of 62.4 years, of whom 43.6% were male. During follow-up, 247 incident AF events (11.1%) were recorded. In fully adjusted models, PRISm was associated with incident AF (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 2.12, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.35–3.31, P = 0.001), and RSP was also associated with incident AF (aOR = 2.38, 95% CI 1.58–3.60, P < 0.001). When participants were categorized into four mutually exclusive groups, PRISm+RSP remained associated with incident AF (aOR = 2.62, 95% CI 1.63–4.22, P < 0.001), whereas PRISm alone (aOR = 0.77, 95% CI 0.21–2.81, P = 0.690) and RSP alone (aOR = 1.88, 95% CI 0.93–3.80, P = 0.077) were not statistically significant. Results were consistent in sensitivity analyses. Among adults without airflow limitation, binary PRISm and RSP were associated with higher odds of incident AF. In mutually exclusive analyses, the clearest association was observed in participants with concurrent reductions in FEV 1 and FVC.

title: Dysregulation of TTN Gene Expression, Titin Protein Levels, and Circulating ncRNAs (miR-200a, lncRNA FOXD2-AS1, and snoRNA-42) in Dilated Cardiomyopathy: A Pilot Study
summary: Dilated Cardiomyopathy is the major cause of congestive heart failure and sudden cardiac death. It is a type of cardiomyopathy characterized by ventricular dilatation, wall thinning and systolic dysfunction. TTN gene is implicated in DCM and encodes for giant titin protein. This study explores the association between TTN gene expression with some types of non-coding RNAs in DCM patients. The study comprised three age- and sex-matched groups (20 individuals each): healthy controls, male patients, and female patients. Relative expression levels of TTN, miR-200a, lncRNA FOXD2-AS1, and snoRNA-42 were quantified using qRT-PCR, whereas serum titin protein levels were measured via ELISA. TTN gene expression was significantly elevated in both male and female DCM patients compared with controls (P<0.001). Furthermore, miR-200a and snoRNA-42 levels were also significantly increased in DCM patients particularly in females. In contrast, lncRNA FOXD2-AS1 was significantly decreased in both sexes of DCM patients. ROC curve analysis for TTN gene demonstrated high diagnostic performance, sensitivity and specificity with (P=0.0022), supporting TTN as a reliable molecular biomarker for DCM. Similarly, miR-200a showed strong diagnostic potential, particularly in females (P=0.0275 in males and P=0.0022 in females), underscoring its efficiency as a sex-specific biomarker. Furthermore, Titin protein level was significantly elevated in DCM patients, particularly in females. Pearson correlation analysis detected a negative correlation between miR-200a and TTN mRNA in both males and females, negative correlations were also observed between miR-200a and titin protein levels. In contrast, TTN gene expression and titin protein levels showed a positive correlation, indicating transcription-driven increases in titin level. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study in Iraq, particularly in Mosul, to integrate Titin protein and TTN gene expression with multiple circulating ncRNA classes (miR-200a, lncRNA FOXD2-AS1 and snoRNA-42) in patients with DCM. The combined analysis of TTN gene / Titin protein axis and ncRNAs within a clinical group from Mosul city provides a comprehensive view of post-transcriptional regulation and revealed sex-dependent molecular differences. Moreover, the strong diagnostic performance of TTN and miR-200a supports their potential as non-invasive biomarkers for DCM. By focusing on a Middle Eastern population, this study contributes novel region-specific molecular data and expands current understanding of DCM beyond previously studied populations. In DCM patients the expression level of TTN gene was significantly increased, demonstrating that transcriptional activation was correlated with myocardial remodeling. The dysregulated expression of ncRNAs (miR-200a, lncRNA FOXD2-AS1 and snoRNA-42), suggested the existence of a complex post-transcriptional regulatory network affecting TTN expression. All of these findings highlight the potential of TTN and ncRNA signatures as promising non-invasive molecular biomarkers for DCM.

title: Vasospastic Angina and Cardiac Arrest
summary: Vasospastic angina (VSA) is an important and potentially treatable cause of cardiac arrest (CA) and may account for approximately 2–10% of otherwise unexplained cases of out-of-hospital CA. VSA can sometimes be diagnosed by spontaneous coronary spasm during emergency coronary angiography or by transient ST-segment elevation during a spontaneous attack after resuscitation. However, because coronary spasm is transient and may not be evident during the initial evaluation, provocation testing after clinical stabilization may be required to establish the diagnosis in otherwise unexplained cases. Once VSA is diagnosed, vasodilator therapy, particularly calcium-channel blockers, is the mainstay of treatment. Nevertheless, survivors of VSA-related CA may remain at risk of recurrent lethal ventricular arrhythmias despite medical therapy. Evaluation for alternative or overlapping arrhythmogenic disorders, including cardiomyopathies and channelopathies, should therefore be considered even after a diagnosis of VSA, and implantable cardioverter-defibrillator implantation may be considered in selected patients according to the risk of recurrence and response to medical therapy. Further prospective studies, including randomized controlled trials, are needed to determine whether systematic provocation testing followed by targeted therapy reduces recurrent ventricular arrhythmias and CA and improves long-term outcomes.

title: Developing a case management program and clinical practice for high-risk sudden cardiac death patients through the lens of family systems theory
summary: Objective To develop a case management plan for patients at high risk of sudden cardiac death (SCD) from the perspective of family systems theory and evaluate its clinical practice effects. Methods By using the random sampling method, 100 patients at high risk of SCD who visited our hospital from March 2025 to June 2025 were selected as the research subjects. They were randomly divided into an experimental group ( n = 50) and a control group ( n = 50). The control group received routine care and follow-up, while the experimental group implemented a case management plan based on the family systems theory, with both interventions lasting for one year. Both groups were evaluated at baseline and endpoint using disease cognition assessments, the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9), Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7), Tampa Scale for Kinesiophobia Heart (TSK-SV Heart), General Self-Efficacy Scale (GSES), Family APGAR, and Major Adverse Cardiac Events (MACE). Results There were no statistically significant differences in baseline data between the two groups ( P > 0.05). After the intervention, the experimental group showed significantly better scores in disease cognition, PHQ-9, GAD-7, TSK-SV Heart, GSES, APGAR, and MACE compared to the control group ( P < 0.05). Conclusion The case management plan for high-risk SCD patients based on family systems theory is scientifically sound and feasible. It can effectively reduce anxiety and depression, alleviate kinesiophobia, improve disease cognition, and promote family care, thereby improving the patients’ quality of life and prognosis.

title: Cardiac screening in the armed forces: bridging policy and practice through expert consensus
summary: Sudden cardiac death in young individuals, though uncommon, remains one of the most devastating events in preventive cardiology. Its occurrence in ostensibly healthy, asymptomatic individuals underscores the limitations of symptom-based risk detection and the need for systematic structured cardiovascular evaluation. This challenge has been recognised across athletic populations, with most sporting bodies and international cardiology societies mandating electrocardiogram (ECG) based cardiac screening in athletes. [1][2][3][4] Sudden cardiac death in military personnel is an equally uncommon but deeply consequential event. Thie incidence of sudden cardiac death appears higher when compared to athletic populations, reported as 6.7-11 per 1000,000 person-years during recruitment and years of service. [5][6][7][8] This reality is even more pertinent in high-hazard occupations, where individuals are routinely exposed to environments and operational demands that amplify cardiovascular strain. This is especially relevant when immediate medical support is not always guaranteed. These environments can unmask latent cardiovascular disease, accelerate physiological stress responses, and convert otherwise survivable arrhythmic events into fatal outcomes. 9 The combination of youth, apparent fitness, and high-risk operational exposure creates a paradoxical vulnerability. Despite these operational concerns, cardiac screening in military recruits is not widespread practice. 10 The European Association of Preventive Cardiology (EAPC) have recently launched a novel, tiered scalable approach to cardiovascular screening in the Armed Forces. 11 These recommendations integrate contemporary scientific evidence with the distinctive realities of military service, balancing operational readiness, logistical constraints, and the early identification of at-risk individuals, while also supporting the physical and mental well being of service members.Sudden death in military personnel is estimated to vary between 6.7-11 per 100,000 person-years. The event rate during recruitment training is equally high, with events often taking place during exercise. Despite these concerning numbers, ECG-based cardiac screening is not widespread practice. In a recent international survey, only 71.4% of countries reported including a resting 12-lead ECG at enrolment. 10 Despite the high reported incidence of sudden cardiac death in new recruits, the diagnostic yield of cardiac screening program in military populations remains poorly defined. [12][13][14][15] Studies describing screening outcomes often employ heterogenous methodologies, retrospective designs, ill-defined denominators, and non-standardized screening protocols.The health of the force is foundational to mission readiness. Cardiac screening protects not only the individual soldier, but the mission, the unit and the operational integrity of the force. Despite this reality, cardiovascular screening across global Armed Forces remains fragmented, shaped by legacy practices rather than contemporary evidence. 10 Cardiac screening is increasingly regarded as a core responsibility rather than a discretionary practice.The proposed screening algorithm for high level athletes have been endorsed by several international societies for several years. [16][17][18][19][20] This is the first attempt by a medical society to propose a uniform cardiac screening protocol for military personnel.The EAPC endorsed proposed structure is both progressive and pragmatic, whilst also acknowledging that not all Military branches have equal access to advanced diagnostics or the relevant cardiology expertise. Such an approach avoids the false dichotomy between no screening and a full cardiac screen. We instead propose a scalable roadmap that can evolve as awareness and resources take shape. 11In this tiered EAPC endorsed screening model, we outline the essential components in a screening program for military personnel. The consensus statement encourages cardiac screening in all new military recruits, thereby acknowledging the seemingly higher risk of SCD during recruitment training. [5][6][7][8] The essential triad of a health questionnaire, physical examination, and resting 12-lead ECG reflects the current screening recommendations for athletic populations (figure 1). The manuscript highlights that a resting ECG is markedly more sensitive than the history or physical examination alone, and that contemporary interpretation criteria have dramatically reduced false positives. 11,21 Extending this to military personnel is not only logical but overdue. This also reflects recent manuscripts supporting ECG based screening models in non-athletic populations. 22,23 Figure 1: Tiered cardiac screening in military personnelThe statement also addresses cardiac screening in older individuals, defined as >40 years of age. The essential triad proposed for younger individuals carries a poor sensitivity to detect atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Coronary artery disease is the leading cause of sudden cardiac death in older individuals, hence why adapting the screening algorithm is essential. 24,25 We also propose incorporating a cardiovascular risk assessment with validated risk scores, 26,27 with ischaemia testing (functional) and/or coronary anatomy testing (coronary anatomy calcium scoring[CACS] or computed tomography coronary angiography [CTCA]) in those with a high or very high cardiovascular risk. This pragmatic approach highlights at risk asymptomatic individuals, whilst safeguarding resources and cost. We do however acknowledge that the optimal method of determining cardiovascular risk in this healthy asymptomatic population remains unclear, especially with emerging evidence of the high prevalence of coronary calcification and high-risk plaque morphology (not flow limiting) in asymptomatic master athletes and military personnel when screened with CACS / CTCA. [28][29][30][31][32][33][34] As outlined in the statement, referral for second line investigations is paramount in those with symptoms, a family history of inherited cardiovascular disorders and/or sudden cardiac death, signs during physical examination and/or ECG abnormalities. 11 Targeted investigations such as echocardiography, exercise testing, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, ambulatory ECG monitoring, CACS/CTCA, are guided by symptoms, abnormal findings, or elevated risk. Infrastructure and expertise play a key role in personalizing the evaluation. Individuals with a diagnosis are then counselled within a multidisciplinary team framework. We also encourage periodic re-evaluation in individuals with early phenotypic traits of cardiovascular disease. 11The shared decision-making model has reshaped exercise recommendations in athletes with cardiovascular disease. Athlete autonomy plays a key role in the process, moving a way from the traditional paternalistic approach. 3,4 Do these concepts apply for military personnel? Cardiovascular readiness has become a defining component of military capability. These individuals are often expected to perform in austere, high stress, and medically remote environments.Individuals with cardiovascular disease exposed to these conditions may inevitably experience symptoms or clinically adverse events. A single event can compromise mission execution, jeopardise colleagues, and erode confidence within tightly bonded units. The consensus statement acknowledges that the shared decision-making model may not be suitable in this unique population, highlighting that a command directed approach is often required to safeguard the individual's safety and the institution's objectives. 11 A recent tactical athletes consensus statement also echoes this proposed shift in practice. 35 The tactical clinical management (TCM) model is a deliberative risk assessment process that factors in the individual's preferences with the realities of operational safety, incorporating task-specific capability, environmental stressors, team and public-safety implications.This novel, tiered screening framework attempts to bring coherence to this military landscape. Its strength lies not only in the scientific rationale but in its pragmatic design. The authors recognize that military organisations differ widely in resources, expertise, and infrastructure. 11 Screening is only as strong as the system that supports it, infrastructure readiness is a prerequisite for implementation (Figure 2). This sentiment is also acknowledged in the recent ACC/AHA scientific statement on Tactical Athletes, 35 novel in its structure, pragmatic in its application, and adaptable across branches and nations. Cardiovascular screening is a strategic necessity that protects is service members whilst strengthens operational capability, aligning military practice with the best available evidence. This is the moment for military organisations to move beyond fragmented legacy approaches, instead adopting a unified, scalable model that ensures service personnel with cardiovascular disease are identified early in their career, managed appropriately, and never left to chance.

title: GCTRNet: global context-gated temporal refinement for short-window ECG-based premature ventricular contraction detection
summary: Background Premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) are one of the most prevalent ventricular arrhythmias and therefore require a method for reliably identifying PVCs from short ECG strips, through an automated system capable of identifying PVCs and evaluating the burden of PVCs. While technology continues to advance, automatic identification of PVCs from very short ECG recordings remains problematic due to significant variability in PVC morphology across various patients as a result of the limited amount of information available from ECG data. Methods To overcome this difficulty, the Global Context-Gated Temporal Refinement (GCTR) module has been created which enhances bidirectional long short-term memory (BLSTM) representations by incorporating segment-level contextual information using context gating and residual learning. The GCTR module was integrated into a convolutional network architecture termed GCTRNet. GCTRNet was evaluated on the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database using a patient-independent partition. The frozen model was further evaluated on a predefined subset of CPSC2021 comprising 210 recordings from 105 patients. Results The frozen seed-2024 model of GCTRNet, when tested on MITDB data, reached an accuracy of 99.65%, a sensitivity of 96.82% and a specificity of 99.91%. The same frozen model achieved performance on the CPSC2021 subset with 97.83% accuracy, 84.75% sensitivity, and 98.11% specificity and an AUPRC of 80.49%. In addition, GCTRNet outperformed matched comparison models based on BLSTM architecture in many metrics of evaluation, thus supporting the potential of the temporal refinement method proposed. Conclusions GCTRNet provides an effective temporal refinement approach for patient-independent short-window PVC detection and shows potential for cross-database application.

title: [Supraventricular tachycardia in advanced age].
Acute lymphocytic myocarditis complicated by bidirectional ventricular tachycardia treated with early steroid use.
summary: Acute lymphocytic myocarditis can precipitate malignant ventricular arrhythmias, including the rare presentation of bidirectional ventricular tachycardia (BDVT), a rhythm associated with significant hemodynamic instability. Although BDVT is classically linked to catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and digitalis toxicity, it is increasingly recognized in myocarditis, likely reflecting diffuse inflammatory involvement of the myocardium and Purkinje system. Emerging evidence suggests that early corticosteroid therapy may rapidly reduce arrhythmia burden and improve ventricular function in selected patients with active myocardial inflammation. We report the case of a 34-year-old woman who presented with palpitations and syncope and was found to have BDVT secondary to acute lymphocytic myocarditis. Despite typical medical management, she had refractory ventricular arrhythmias. Prompt initiation of corticosteroids led to marked suppression of arrhythmias and rapid recovery of left ventricular ejection fraction. While current data remain limited, this case supports the potential benefit of early immunosuppressive therapy when active lymphocytic inflammation is strongly suspected.

title: Frontiers in the Risk Stratification and Prevention of Sudden Cardiac Arrest and Death in Athletes
summary: Background: Sudden cardiac arrest (SCA) and sudden cardiac death (SCD) remain the leading causes of exercise-related mortality in athletes. Research in recent years has produced substantial advances in the understanding of athlete-specific risk, the etiologic spectrum of SCA/SCD, and the tools available for screening and risk stratification. Methods: We performed a narrative review of the literature identified through PubMed/MEDLINE searches of related terms, supplemented by targeted searches and reference checking. Summary of the Review: In this narrative review, we synthesize updated evidence on the epidemiology, etiologies, screening, and emerging technologies relevant to SCA/SCD in athletes. Conclusions: Contemporary evaluation of SCA/SCD risk in athletes relies on multimodal, individualized assessment with longitudinal surveillance and shared decision-making. Emerging computational tools may further refine risk prediction, but current evidence remains limited.

title: Hidden and Atypical Presentations of Myocarditis in Sudden Cardiac Death: A Narrative Review.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Myocarditis is an inflammatory disease of the heart muscle, presenting from asymptomatic cases to sudden cardiac death. Its diagnosis is challenging, especially when classic cardiac symptoms are absent presents with unusual manifestations. Recognition of these unusual manifestations is essential to prevent sudden death and increase clinical awareness.

METHODS: This narrative review was conducted to summarize the evidence on myocarditis with occult and nonclassical manifestations and its role in sudden cardiac death. A systematic search was performed in PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar for studies published between 2000 and 2025. Search terms included English language, such as "myocarditis," "sudden cardiac death," "atypical presentation," "silent myocarditis," and "gastrointestinal symptoms".

RESULTS: A total of 10 studies were included and analyzed, focusing on clinical characteristics, nonclassical presentations, diagnostic findings, and outcomes. Myocarditis can be insidious and asymptomatic in young patients and increases the risk of sudden cardiac death. The diagnosis of these cases is often only possible after cardiac arrest or autopsy. In addition, myocarditis may present with nonclassical symptoms, particularly gastrointestinal symptoms, delaying diagnosis.

CONCLUSION: Myocarditis, whether asymptomatic or with nonclassical manifestations such as gastrointestinal symptoms, can be a serious health threat, especially in young people, and in some cases can cause sudden cardiac death. Evidence suggests that many of these deaths in apparently healthy individuals are due to undiagnosed myocarditis. Early recognition and attention to nonclassical symptoms are essential to prevent sudden death and improve patient management.

title: Coronary stent fixation of left ventricular lead during CRT-D implantation: a case series of three patients
summary: Objective To investigate a salvage method using coronary stent fixation of the left ventricular (LV) lead to manage refractory LV lead dislodgement caused by unfavorable coronary venous anatomy during cardiac resynchronization therapy defibrillator (CRT-D) implantation, and to evaluate its technical feasibility and clinical value. Methods We retrospectively included three patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) at our center who developed LV lead dislodgement during or early after CRT-D implantation. Conventional methods failed to maintain a stable lead position. A sirolimus-eluting coronary stent was deployed within the target coronary vein to achieve mechanical anchoring of the LV lead via gentle compression against the venous wall. Procedural details, perioperative complications, and follow-up data were collected and analyzed. Results All three patients completed stent fixation of the LV lead. No acute severe complications, such as coronary venous rupture, pericardial tamponade, or lead conductor damage, occurred intraoperatively. No significant change in pacing threshold was observed before and after stent deployment. Cases 1 and 2 were followed for 30 and 26 months, respectively, and lead parameters remained stable. Case 3 was followed for only 2 months and then lost to follow-up; lead parameters were stable at that time point. No clinically meaningful improvement in LV ejection fraction (LVEF) was observed in Cases 1 and 2 during follow-up. Because Case 3 was followed for only 2 months, shorter than the usual 6–12-month window for assessing CRT reverse remodeling, functional response could not be evaluated. This procedure constitutes off-label device use; after full stent deployment, the lead position cannot be readjusted. If device-related infection occurs, transvenous lead extraction may be difficult and uncertain, and surgical removal may be required. Conclusions After all conventional methods have failed, stent fixation may serve as a salvage option for refractory LV lead dislodgement caused by unfavorable coronary venous anatomy. This report describes the clinical observations of sirolimus-eluting stent use in this off-label salvage procedure and details the relevant procedural parameters and techniques. However, the sample size is small, and potential long-term risks, including stent fracture, lead insulation damage, and stability of lead electrical parameters, require further evaluation in larger studies. This technique only addresses the mechanical fixation of the lead and does not guarantee functional benefit from CRT.

title: Circadian timing does not modulate human temporal contrast sensitivity.
summary: Previous studies have reported diurnal variations in color perception and luminance contrast sensitivity, suggesting modulation of visual processing by the circadian pacemaker. To clarify potential time-of-day effects, we examined whether cone-mediated temporal contrast sensitivity is modulated by circadian timing. We disentangled circadian and homeostatic influences on human visual performance using a 40-hour forced desynchrony protocol. Twelve participants (five female participants, 24.4 ± 2.9 years, range 19-30) followed a repeating 3.75-hour cycle comprising 2 hours 30 minutes of wakefulness and 1 hour 15 minutes of sleep under constant environmental conditions. Circadian period was estimated from up to 46 salivary melatonin samples per participant. During wake periods, participants repeatedly completed temporal contrast sensitivity tasks at 2 Hz and 8 Hz, using tasks that probed both luminance (L+M+S) and chromatic (L-M, S-cone-directed) modulations. We tested for circadian modulation of visual performance by comparing hierarchical cosinor models with intercept-only null models using Bayes factors. All participants showed robust melatonin rhythms (mean τ = 24.18 ± 0.39 hours). Bayesian inference provided decisive evidence against circadian variation in luminance or chromatic contrast sensitivity. Within this controlled protocol, we found no detectable near-24-hour modulation of cone-mediated temporal contrast sensitivity. Previously reported time-of-day effects may instead reflect homeostatic influences, pupil-linked changes in retinal illuminance, or mechanisms outside the cone-mediated pathways probed here. By separating circadian phase from sleep-wake-related influences, this study clarifies when circadian modulation of visual performance can and cannot be inferred.

title: Leadless Pacemakers After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement: A Meta-analysis With Time-to-Event Analysis.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Permanent pacemaker implantation is a common complication after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). Leadless pacemakers (LPs) may reduce lead- and pocket-related complications, but their clinical outcomes after TAVR remain uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the safety and effectiveness of LPs compared with transvenous pacemakers (TVPs).

METHODS: PubMed, Scopus, and ScienceDirect were searched from inception to June 10, 2026. Randomized and observational studies were included. Random-effects meta-analyses pooled proportions, risk ratios (RRs), and mean differences (MDs). Reconstructed Kaplan-Meier data were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs).

RESULTS: Ten studies involving 10,809 patients (1030 LP and 9779 TVP recipients) were included. The pooled procedural success rate of LP implantation was 98% (95% CI 95%-99%). Implantation success was comparable between LP and TVP (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.98-1.02). Sensitivity analysis demonstrated a shorter hospital stay with LP (MD -1.37 days, 95% CI -2.33 to -0.41) and a lower risk of heart failure hospitalization (RR 0.37, 95% CI 0.14-0.96). Overall survival did not differ between groups (HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.44-1.23), although reconstructed survival curves showed late separation favoring LP. Device-related and vascular complications were comparable between LP and TVP.

CONCLUSIONS: LP implantation after TAVR demonstrates excellent procedural success and clinical outcomes comparable to TVPs. LPs may reduce hospital stay and heart failure hospitalization, supporting their use as an alternative pacing strategy in appropriately selected patients.

title: Pathogenesis, screening, and diagnosis of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
summary: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a common heritable heart disease. The disease is genetically, anatomically, and clinically heterogeneous. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern but has allelic heterogeneity, incomplete penetrance, and variable expressivity. Beyond family screening, clinical evaluation for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is often prompted by identification of symptoms or detection of a heart murmur, additionally, abnormal electrocardiogram or imaging results performed for another reason can provide evidence. Evaluation should include obtaining a patient's history, a physical examination, cardiac imaging, and, often, genetic testing. Prognosis is variable; major causes of morbidity and mortality are caused by sudden cardiac death, heart failure, and atrial fibrillation with associated stroke risk. An understanding of the pathogenesis at the genetic, cellular, and individual levels helps clinicians to implement appropriate screening, recognise clinical manifestations, and improve the treatment of patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The understanding of this condition is evolving, with recent advances and insights into its pathogenesis, refinement of risk stratification, and use of artificial intelligence in screening, diagnosis, and prognostication.

title: Nox4 Mediates Diastolic Function in a Genetic Model of Pitx2 Haploinsufficiency.
summary: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) commonly coexists with atrial fibrillation (AF), but shared mechanisms remain unclear. In this study, we hypothesized that Pitx2, a transcription factor located near the strongest genetic locus associated with AF in humans, increases susceptibility to HFpEF-like remodeling. We also sought to understand pathways that might be central to this increased risk. Male and female Pitx2+/- mice and wild-type littermates received 3-week subcutaneous osmotic pump infusion of saline or angiotensin II (Ang II; 500 ng/kg/min). Cardiac structure and function were assessed by echocardiography and catheterization, and functional capacity by exercise treadmill. RNA transcriptomic profiling was performed to identify candidate pathways. In a separate cohort, Ang II-treated mice were randomized to oral GKT136901 (30 mg/kg/day) or vehicle during infusion. After Ang II infusion, Pitx2+/- mice developed exaggerated HFpEF-like changes, including greater left ventricular hypertrophy, left atrial enlargement, diastolic dysfunction, elevated left ventricular end-diastolic pressure, and reduced treadmill performance. RNA-seq showed enrichment of metabolic and stress-response pathways with selective upregulation of Nox4, confirmed by RT-qPCR. GKT136901 attenuated structural remodeling, diastolic dysfunction indices, elevated filling pressures, and cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, but did not improve endurance. These findings implicate redox signaling, including Nox4, in AF genetic susceptibility-HFpEF interactions.

title: A scalable segment-based in vivo platform for precision modeling of dilated and hypertrophic cardiomyopathies in Drosophila
summary: Cardiomyopathies are major causes of heart failure and sudden cardiac death, yet the functional consequences of many disease-associated genes and variants remain poorly defined. Here, we establish a scalable, segment-based in vivo platform in Drosophila for quantitative cardiac phenotyping and precision modeling of cardiomyopathy subtypes. By integrating established cardiac imaging approaches into a standardized framework, termed Segmental Cardiac Output and Performance Evaluation (SCOPE), we systematically compared cardiac function across abdominal heart segments. This analysis identified segment A3 as the dominant pumping region, exhibiting the largest systolic and diastolic diameters, highest fractional shortening, and greatest cardiac output, thereby providing an optimal and reproducible site for functional assessment. Leveraging this platform, we generated genetically defined models of dilated and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy through heart-specific knockdown of LamC and bt , homologs of human LMNA and MYBPC3 , respectively. LamC silencing produced hallmark features of dilated cardiomyopathy, including chamber dilation, cardiomyocyte loss, reduced contractility, and decreased cardiac output. In contrast, bt silencing induced hypertrophic remodeling characterized by increased heart wall thickness and impaired cardiac performance. These models recapitulate key structural and functional characteristics of human cardiomyopathy subtypes. Together, this work establishes a scalable in vivo platform for segment-resolved cardiac phenotyping that enables precise modeling of cardiomyopathy, systematic functional validation of candidate genes and variants, and future discovery of genetic and pharmacologic modifiers.

title: Bone Morphogenetic Protein-10 as a Predictor of Atrial Fibrillation Recurrence After Catheter Ablation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Biomarkers of atrial cardiomyopathy may improve the prediction of recurrence of atrial fibrillation (AF) after catheter ablation. Bone morphogenetic protein-10 (BMP10) is an atrial-specific cardiomyocyte protein and a potential biomarker, but evidence is limited and not comprehensively synthesized.

METHODS: We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies to evaluate the association between circulating BMP10 concentrations with AF recurrence after catheter ablation. Pooled hazard ratios (HRs) with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were computed using a random-effects model. The primary analysis used unadjusted HRs per continuous BMP10 levels from all included studies. Secondary analyses were conducted based on the adjusted HRs of studies with continuous BMP10 and all studies, including one study that reported adjusted HRs based on quartiles.

RESULTS: Three studies were included. In the primary analysis without adjustment (n = 3), increased levels of BMP10 were significantly associated with recurrence of AF (pooled HR 1.53, 95% CI 1.13-2.07; P = 0.006), with moderate-to-high heterogeneity (I2 = 69%). The association was attenuated and non-significant in the adjusted analysis of two studies with continuous BMP10 (HR 1.46, 95% CI 0.94-2.25; I2 = 59%). However, after the inclusion of a third study with adjusted quartile-based HR, the statistical significance was re-demonstrated (HR 1.33, 95% CI 1.16-1.53; P < 0.001) with low heterogeneity (I2 = 20%).

CONCLUSION: Elevated BMP10 levels are correlated with higher risk of AF recurrence following catheter ablation. Although the results are consistent across analyses, they should be interpreted with caution due to the small number of studies and methodological heterogeneity. BMP10 needs to be confirmed as a clinically applicable biomarker by larger prospective studies.

title: The internal-to-external validation gap in AI-ECG diagnostic models: protocol and amendments of a systematic review and meta-analysis
summary: This registration archives the protocol (version 2.6, dated 21 July 2026) of a systematic review and meta-analysis that estimates, for artificial-intelligence electrocardiogram (AI-ECG) diagnostic models, the paired difference in discrimination between internal and external validation cohorts: internal minus external logit(AUROC), paired within study, model, target and external cohort. The primary inferential quantity is the 95% prediction interval of that gap across the literature. It also archives every amendment adopted under protocol section 17 to date, each dated in its own file: irreconcilable tier-1 printings (section 17.4); a scoped CI-ceiling calculation exception; the primary heterogeneity hierarchy (random effects for clusters and pairs within clusters, sampling covariance for shared estimates, CR2 cluster-robust inference with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom); and the plan of a preliminary analysis for a congress abstract: versions 1, 2 and 4 (2 October 2026) and versions 5 and 7 (3 October 2026). Version 5 records rulings made after an independent review of the first preliminary run: pairs whose external validation fails a protocol question on label integrity are excluded (section 15.13), independence clusters are corrected from the articles, several values are corrected from the articles, and the protocol's anchored probability of degradation and reporting-completeness test are added. Version 7 is the governing version; it corrects two internal inconsistencies of version 5 before any result of the corresponding run. Versions 3 and 6 are held in the project archive (version 3 had a formatting error; version 6 differs from version 7 only in quoting a value in its exposure statement, which this public record omits). The deviation record PD-06, with its addendum of 3 October 2026, lists the protocol sections that the preliminary analysis does not yet meet. One rule of the abstract figure was set after the independent verification of the preliminary analysis had been computed and before the run that produces the abstract (decision DP-96 in the project's decision log): the 95% prediction band is drawn only where its Satterthwaite degrees of freedom are at least 5, as protocol section 13.2.4 requires for any inference; the curve of predicted values is drawn over the whole range. Plan version 7, section 10, does not state this condition. Timing statement. This registration is made after data extraction began, after pilot analyses that the protocol itself declares (section 13.3) and after a first preliminary analysis. It is not a prospective registration; it is a time-stamped record of the protocol and its amendments. Each plan version states what had been computed and seen when it was written.
